source: Lombrozo (2007) Simplicity and probability in causal explanation, Cognitive Psychology 55:232-257 (Exp 1)
finding: With no probability information people pick the explanation with fewer causes. With base rates given they pick the more probable one. Both are real virtues.
numbers: Exp 1, N=48 undergraduates, between subjects. Simplicity condition: 96% chose the one-cause explanation. Probability condition: 92% chose the explanation with the more common disease. Justifications: of simple-choosers, 17% cited simplicity itself, 39% sufficiency, 39% probability.
limits: Alien-disease vignettes, student sample, forced choice. Participants may assume equal base rates, which makes the single cause genuinely more likely (the paper tests this in Exp 2).
agent_relevance: A simplicity preference is partly a hidden probability judgment. If the agent ranks explanations, simplicity must be an explicit scored feature, not a vibe.

source: Lombrozo (2007) Exp 2 (simplicity vs probability trade-off)
finding: When base rates are given, people still favor the simpler explanation more than Bayes allows. The bias acts like a high prior on the simple explanation, not a wrong use of the data.
numbers: N=144, 8 base-rate conditions, 18 per cell. 71% chose the simple explanation overall. Choice depended on base rate, chi2(7)=25, p<.01. Even when the two-cause option was 10 times more likely, over a third chose the simple one. Logistic fit: slope .795 (not different from 1, so probability weighted correctly), constant -1.306 (p<.01). Implied prior factor about 4 for the simple explanation (CI 2.3 to 6), prior about 79% (69-86%). 69% passed a joint-probability check question.
limits: Between-subjects aggregate fit, not a per-person model. 17 participants were flagged as misunderstanding; the slope held when they were dropped.
agent_relevance: Gives a size for the simplicity bias (about 4:1 prior). A scaffold that uses 'prefer the simpler hypothesis' should treat it as a prior to be overridden by evidence, with a known size.

source: Lombrozo (2007) Exp 3 (experienced frequencies) and overestimation result
finding: Replication with frequencies learned by experience instead of stated numbers. The simplicity bias shrank but stayed. People who commit to an unlikely simple explanation then overestimate how common its cause is.
numbers: N=108, 4 base-rate conditions, 27 each. 63% chose the simple explanation overall. At a 1:10 ratio against it, 41% still did (39% in Exp 2). Slope .62, constant -.77, implied prior 68% (57-78%), constant lower than Exp 2 (p<.05). At the 9:10 ratio fewer chose it than in Exp 2: 59% vs 89% (chi2(1)=4.6, p<.05). Overestimation of the chosen disease's prevalence: F(1,50)=7.93, p<.01.
limits: The overestimation effect is the main evidence that choosing an explanation changes later belief; the paper discusses a frequency-estimation confound and argues against it.
agent_relevance: Choosing an explanation can distort later probability estimates. Supports G4 and the rule to keep hypotheses separate from the credences assigned to them, and to re-score from data not from memory of the choice.

source: Lombrozo (2007) Exp 4 (probability made unambiguous)
finding: The simplicity preference mostly disappears when the joint probability of the complex explanation is shown directly. Asking for the 'most likely' explanation instead of the 'most satisfying' one moves answers only partly.
numbers: N=48. Joint-probability condition: 17% chose the simple explanation, versus 61% at the matching 2:3 ratio in Exp 2 (chi2(1)=8.85, p<.01). 'Most likely' wording: 46% chose simple (vs 17%, chi2(1)=4.75, p<.05; vs 61%, n.s.). Math-check correct: 75%.
limits: Small N per cell. Shows the preference is a default under uncertainty about probability, not a fixed taste.
agent_relevance: Intervention with a big effect: put the explicit probabilities in front of the judge and the simplicity bias falls from 61% to 17%. A scaffold step 'write the joint likelihood of each rival' should do the same.

source: Liquin & Lombrozo (2018) Causal structure and probability information modulate the preference for simple explanations, CogSci proceedings
finding: Simplicity preference depends on causal structure. It is strongest when one cause explains two independent effects, modest for jointly sufficient causes, and reverses (favors the complex explanation) for independently sufficient causes. With base rates and likelihoods matched, simplicity preferences shrink and some flip.
numbers: N=544 adults, one simple and one complex explanation under one of three causal structures. Only the abstract page (1 page) was available; effect sizes not read.
quote: simplicity preferences are moderated by several factors
limits: Abstract only. The year is inferred from the proceedings and the cited works. Details of effect sizes not verified.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition: 'fewer causes wins' is not universal. A rule favoring the shortest explanation will be wrong when causes are independently sufficient.

source: Douven & Schupbach (2015) Probabilistic alternatives to Bayesianism: the case of explanationism, Frontiers in Psychology 6:459
finding: Reanalysis of an urn experiment: people's credences after each draw are predicted better when their own judgments of explanatory goodness are added to the Bayesian posterior. So explanatory considerations enter human updating.
numbers: Data from Schupbach (2011): 26 participants, two urns of 40 balls (30 black/10 white vs 15 black/25 white), 10 draws, credence and explanatory-goodness ratings after each draw. Bayesian-only model MO: R2=0.83, AIC -398.77. Explanationist model MOAB (adds goodness of both hypotheses): R2=0.90; AIC difference over 120 in its favor; likelihood-ratio statistic 124.87, p<0.0001. Models using computed explanatory-power measures (Popper, Good and others) also beat MO, e.g. MOAP BP AIC -435.27, R2=0.85.
quote: our results weigh against the generality of the increasingly popular hypothesis that people tend to update by means of Bayes's Rule
limits: Authors call the context 'rather special'. Small N. Fit to people's credences, not accuracy against truth. Explanatory-goodness ratings are themselves partly driven by likelihood, so the extra predictors may encode probability the O term misses.
agent_relevance: Humans combine probability and explanatory goodness. An LLM trained on human text may inherit this. Do not assume model confidences are Bayesian; calibrate them against checks.

source: Douven & Schupbach (2015), normative section, summarizing Douven (2013) simulation
finding: In a coin-bias simulation, an explanationist update (a bonus to the best-explaining hypothesis) reaches a high probability on the true bias much faster than Bayes's rule. The authors argue speed can offset Dutch-book exposure and that no argument shows accuracy minimization in the Bayesian sense is the only goal.
numbers: No new numbers in this paper; the speed result is reported secondhand from Douven (2013). The text says 'virtually always much faster' to reach a high-probability threshold.
limits: Secondhand. Speed is bought with a worse long-run Brier score (see b08). The comparison depends on the bonus size and the setting.
agent_relevance: Support for an 'explanation bonus' as a way to commit sooner. Only useful when waiting is costly; the price is more error in the long run.

source: Trpin & Pellert (2019) Inference to the best explanation in uncertain evidential situations, BJPS 70(4):978-1001
finding: Extends the explanationist update to uncertain evidence (rule IBE**) and compares it with Jeffrey conditionalization in coin-bias simulations. IBE** more often puts high probability on the true bias, gets there faster, and gives more accurate distributions.
numbers: Catalogue page and abstract only. No simulation numbers in what was opened.
limits: Abstract-level only. A thesis summary seen in search says the explanationist is faster but slightly worse on Brier score under certain evidence; the accuracy advantage is parameter and setting dependent. That secondary claim was not opened.
agent_relevance: Same message as b07: a bonus helps under noisy evidence, which is the usual case for an LLM reading a messy tool output.

source: Dalal, Valentino, Freitas, Buitelaar (2024/2025) Inference to the Best Explanation in Large Language Models (IBE-Eval), ACL 2024; arXiv 2402.10767v2
finding: Scores competing LLM-written explanations with four features taken from IBE theory: consistency, parsimony, coherence, linguistic uncertainty. The combined score picks the more plausible explanation better than a GPT-3.5 judge.
numbers: Causal QA on COPA and E-CARE with GPT-3.5, Llama 2 7B and 13B. Up to 77% accuracy (27 points above random), +17 points over GPT-3.5-as-judge (average +17.5). Spearman with human judgment 0.64 (p<0.01) for IBE-Eval vs 0.31 (not significant) for the GPT-3.5 judge. Cohen's kappa 0.68 between two human evaluators.
limits: Two-choice causal QA, small models, explanations written by the same model that is scored. Each single criterion is weak alone.
agent_relevance: Code-computed explanation features beat a model judge (supports G5). Use features, not an LLM opinion, to rank rival explanations.

source: Dalal et al. (2024) IBE-Eval, per-criterion results
finding: Consistency is nearly useless: LLMs can build a logically consistent story for any option, and over-rationalize wrong ones by adding premises. Parsimony and coherence are better. Hedging language (uncertainty) is the strongest single signal.
numbers: Proof depth and concept drift were on average 6% and 10% greater for the incorrect option. Parsimony beat consistency by an average of 14% in predictive power. Uncertainty features added 13 percentage points on COPA and 4 on E-CARE. Larger models over-rationalized more: the depth and drift gap was greatest for GPT-3.5.
limits: Hedge words track plausibility only as the model itself feels it; this may fail for confident wrong answers. Linear regression on few features.
agent_relevance: Warning for generate-then-test: a story that fits the facts is cheap. Fit is not evidence. Tie to G3: the test must be on something the explanation was not fitted to.

source: Sun & Saparov (2026) Do Language Models Follow Occam's Razor? Parsimony in inductive and abductive reasoning (InAbHyD), arXiv 2509.03345v2
finding: Synthetic first-order-logic task: given an incomplete ontology and observations, propose hypotheses. Models are fine with one hypothesis and a shallow tree, then collapse as the tree grows or several hypotheses must work together. 'Weak accuracy' (any correct hypothesis) stays much higher than 'strong accuracy' and 'quality' (correct and simplest).
numbers: Single hypothesis, tree height 1: every model above 80%. Multi-hypothesis, height 1 to 2: accuracy falls from above 80% to below 50% for all models except GPT-4o, though true hypotheses only rise from 3.0 to 3.5. Models: GPT-5.4, o3, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemma3-27B, Llama3-70B, DeepSeek-R1-distill-Llama-70B. Height 4: all models reach at least 20% weak accuracy but very low strong accuracy and quality. Their quality metric agreed with human annotation 79% of the time (random 33.3%, length baseline 51%).
limits: Synthetic ontology worlds; Occam metric defined by the authors.
agent_relevance: The failure is picking the parsimonious set, not producing a plausible one. Add a code step that measures hypothesis size and checks that every observation is covered with the fewest assumptions.

source: Sun & Saparov (2026) InAbHyD, interventions
finding: Few-shot examples help only when they match the test difficulty. Reasoning models and buffer-of-thought prompts help but do not close the gap between weak and strong accuracy.
numbers: 8 demonstrations with chain-of-thought. In-distribution demos (same tree height) improved strong accuracy and quality at heights 3 and 4. Out-of-distribution demos (height 1 only): no significant gain. GPT-5.4 and o3 beat Llama3-70B at all heights. Buffer-of-thought beat chain-of-thought, mostly on weak accuracy. 200 failed responses were hand-coded into four error types.
limits: Figures only for most values; exact percentages were not tabulated in the text.
agent_relevance: Examples at easy depth do not teach hard abduction. Use worked examples at the target depth, or skip them. More reasoning does not fix the choice of the simplest set.

source: Abe et al. (2026) Abductive Reasoning with Syllogistic Forms in Large Language Models, arXiv 2603.06428
finding: Turning a syllogism set into abduction tasks shows LLMs are much worse at abduction than deduction on the same content. They show human-like belief bias, and they almost never answer 'neither is a good explanation'.
numbers: n=216 items per task. Zero-shot overall accuracy on abduction: GPT-4 41.67%, GPT-3.5 31.02%, Llama3-8B 37.50%, Llama3-70B 37.04%. Deduction zero-shot: GPT-4 72.22%. GPT-4 abduction accuracy on the 'Neither' answer: 0.00% zero-shot; 2.78% few-shot. Belief-inconsistent items about 10 points lower than consistent in GPT-4 zero-shot (34.85 vs 46.97). Few-shot helped only Llama-3-70B on abduction: 75.46% overall, 62.96% on Neither, yet below its deduction score of 84.72%. GPT-4 few-shot abduction fell to 28.70% while its few-shot deduction rose to 95.83%.
limits: 2023-era models (gpt-4-0613, gpt-3.5-turbo-0125, Llama 3). Heavy answer-type bias: GPT-4 picked the Negative option 67.9% of the time while the true rate was 16.7%. Few-shot instability suggests prompt sensitivity.
agent_relevance: Models rarely say 'none of these explains it'. A scaffold needs an explicit 'no candidate adequate' exit that code can trigger, and should not rely on few-shot to teach it.

source: Steiglechner, Mahler & Lohmann (2026) LLMs Can See the Smoke but not the Fire: Evaluating Abductive Reasoning with Elenchos, arXiv 2607.12733
finding: Models notice that a rule system has been changed but cannot name which change did it. Accuracy collapses once there are two or more changes, and nearly to zero when the changes interact. Extra reasoning budget did not help consistently.
numbers: 13 LLMs in the 'Ladder' study. Kernel detection accuracy 0.65 vs exact mutation attribution 0.28. Wide panel of 30 LLMs: exact accuracy 0.90 (k=0), 0.32 (k=1), 0.15 (k=2+), 0.15 (k=3+), and 0.03 for interacting sets; hardest cell 0.02. In 86.5% of cases with right detection but wrong attribution, the probe budget was left unused. If the model was told k, it tended to invent mutations to fill slots; if not told, it omitted some.
limits: Compute-scaling result is explicitly preliminary: one configuration, n=5 per model and effort level. Formal lambda-calculus-style systems, not natural science.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G1 and for forcing tests before commit: models stop probing while still wrong. Also warns that stating how many causes exist pushes the model to fabricate causes.

source: Steiglechner et al. (2026) Elenchos, prompt-information effect
finding: Giving structural hints in the system prompt is what lets weaker models score at all. Performance falls steadily as hints are removed.
numbers: Random baselines: 1/13 (0.077) for one mutation, 1/64 (0.016) for two, 1/3 for kernel choice. Weaker models fail almost completely without strong prompt scaffolding. At k=2 with the lowest-information prompt and interacting mutations, only gpt-5.4_medium (0.20) and gpt-5.4 (0.07) scored above zero; the highest reasoning setting scored 0.
limits: Per-model cells have few runs; read them as direction, not size.
agent_relevance: Scaffold information (what kinds of explanation are allowed, ontology) matters more than extra thinking time for abduction. Matches our approach of building the scaffold rather than the model.

source: Survey 'Wiring the Why' (2026) Unified taxonomy and survey of abductive reasoning in LLMs, with benchmark study (Table 3, 4), arXiv 2604.08016v2
finding: Selecting among given explanations is nearly solved on short commonsense tasks, but long-narrative and open-ended settings are still below humans. Splitting abduction into generation (stage I) and selection (stage II) shows generation is harder.
numbers: Selection accuracy, GPT-5.4: ART 87.2 (human 91.4), e-CARE 88.0 (human 92.0), True Detective 42.9 (human average 47.0), MuSR murder 60.8 (GPT-4o best at 68.0, human 92.1). DDXPlus diagnosis ranking: Top-1 79.75, Hit@3 98.7. The same diagnosis task as open generation: Hit@3 63.0, Set-F1@3 28.1. Generation: ProofWriter best 21.5% exact, AbductionRules 99.6, UNcommonsense win rate 61.5 (GPT-5.4) vs 41.0 (Llama3.3-70B).
limits: Within-suite comparison only: subsets, and several generation metrics use LLM judges, so do not compare with published scores. ART and e-CARE gap is harder to read since the two stages use different metrics.
agent_relevance: Ranking candidates is cheap, producing the right candidate is the bottleneck. Spend budget on diverse generation and verified selection, not on better judging.

source: Del & Fishel (2023) True Detective: a deep abductive reasoning benchmark undoable for GPT-3 and challenging for GPT-4, arXiv 2212.10114
finding: Detective puzzles of over 1000 words with 3 to 5 suspects. Vanilla and chain-of-thought prompting stay near chance. Handing the model a gold reasoning chain lifts GPT-4 to 83%, showing that producing the explanation, not the final pick, is the weak step.
numbers: 191 puzzles, random 24%, human average 47% (about 2000 attempts per puzzle; top ten humans 80-90%). Vanilla: GPT-3.5 FeedME 28%, GPT-3.5 PPO 26%, GPT-4 27%. Chain of thought: 26%, 29%, GPT-4 38%. Golden chain of thought: GPT-3.5 FeedME 46%, PPO 63%, GPT-4 83%. GPT-4 successes correlate with puzzles that are easy for humans.
limits: 2022-23 models, GPT only. Gold chains of thought give away the answer path, so this is an upper bound of the pick-the-culprit step.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as b16 from another angle: given the right explanation, the model infers well. The search over explanations is where an external loop must help.

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber, Goodman (2024) Hypothesis Search: inductive reasoning with language models, ICLR 2024; arXiv 2309.05660
finding: Generate many natural-language hypotheses, turn each into a program, test on the given examples, run feedback loops. This beats direct prompting on ARC and other rule-finding tasks. The measured bottleneck is getting a correct hypothesis into the candidate set.
numbers: ARC, random 100 tasks, GPT-4: direct 17%; programs only 23%; LLM-summarized hypotheses 30%; human-selected hypotheses 33%; human-written (LARC) hypotheses 45%. GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis (64 samples) for 49 tasks; 28 of the 30 tasks solved with summaries had a correct hypothesis before summarizing; 33 of 49 (67%) human-selected ones became correct programs. Execution feedback: 24 to 30 over 0 to 3 rounds, then plateau. 1D-ARC (108 tasks): programs only 61.1, full 73.1. List Functions: direct 31, programs only 59, full 69. SyGuS: 94.3 with or without hypotheses. Icecuber (no LLM) 43%.
limits: Chain-of-thought without programs scored 19% regardless of hypothesis source. Value of the hypothesis step depends on task: on SyGuS it added nothing. Passing training examples can still mean a wrong hypothesis (our own ARC data shows this).
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for generate-then-test with a code executor. Gain from hypotheses (23 to 30) is real but smaller than from running code (17 to 23) and from a human-quality hypothesis (45).

source: He, Wu, Zhang, Wan, Zhao, Du, Chen (2025) GEAR: a general evaluation framework for abductive reasoning, arXiv 2509.24096
finding: Scores sets of hypotheses by code: consistency with observations, generalization to unseen inputs, and diversity. Most generated hypotheses fail the consistency check, and gold-answer benchmarks wrongly penalize equally valid explanations.
numbers: 9 LLMs, 4 benchmarks, 1,500 problems, 50,340 hypotheses: 17,835 consistent (35%), 28,159 contradicted an observation, 4,346 broke the format. The paper states 70B-class models give only about 20% consistent hypotheses. Consistency not significantly related to the number of initial observations. Model size weakly related to diversity. Around 80% of equally plausible hypotheses are marked incorrect by gold-label evaluation.
limits: Program-style tasks (Mini-ARC, ACRE, List Functions, ARC-2025) where hypotheses can be executed. The two consistency figures (35% overall, 20% for 70B-class) were not reconciled in the text.
agent_relevance: Underdetermination is the norm. Rank hypotheses by code-run consistency and held-out prediction, and keep several distinct survivors instead of one 'best'.

source: GEAR (2025) training result
finding: Training on label-free GEAR signals raises consistency, generalization and diversity, and the gains show on older gold-label abduction benchmarks.
numbers: Preference-RL with LoRA on Qwen-2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, NextCoder-7B with a momentum curriculum. A training figure reports roughly 60% validation accuracy on the GEAR preference. Exact benchmark deltas were not read.
limits: Exact transfer gains not extracted. Training is outside our scaffold-only scope.
agent_relevance: Shows the three GEAR measures can be computed without labels; usable as test-time selectors even if we do not train.

source: Kim (2022) Can language models perform abductive commonsense reasoning? (course report on aNLI/aNLG), arXiv 2207.05155
finding: Student review and re-implementation of aNLG baselines (GPT-2 with or without commonsense inputs and constrained decoding). Notes models are weak at negation and often copy observations.
numbers: Re-implemented GPT-2 variants scored low on BLEU (around 3 to 4) and higher on BERTScore (around 48 to 49) in the table; columns were not cleanly extractable.
limits: Unreviewed report, GPT-2 era. Useful only as a note that automatic overlap metrics hardly reflect explanation quality.
agent_relevance: Low. Confirms that string-overlap metrics are poor for explanations; use execution checks instead.

source: Schupbach and the Bayesian-IBE simulations as summarized in a review (metapsychology.net, ?p=8055)
finding: Search snippet: simulations find IBE does almost as well as Bayes when priors are accurate, and may be more reliable when priors are inaccurate.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Search snippet only; not opened. Treat as unverified. Read Schupbach's simulation paper before using.
agent_relevance: If it holds, an explanation bonus is a cheap guard against a bad prior, which is the usual case for an LLM with a weak prior on a new task.

source: Climenhaga (2017) Inference to the Best Explanation made incoherent, Journal of Philosophy
finding: Search snippet: argues that non-Bayesian IBE as a full-belief rule produces inconsistent beliefs, and as an updating rule produces incoherent credences, using cases with several levels of explanation.
numbers: None.
limits: Snippet only. A rival to the explanationist simulations in b06 to b08.
agent_relevance: Why not to let an explanation bonus change stored probabilities silently; keep the bonus as a selection rule, kept apart from credence.

source: Cabrera (2017) Can there be a Bayesian explanationism? On the prospects of a productive partnership, Synthese
finding: Search snippet: many listed explanatory virtues lack confirmational import; some are 'informational' virtues that add content without raising probability against rivals.
numbers: None.
limits: Snippet only. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Which virtues to score and which to ignore. Candidates for our scored list: consistency with data and held-out prediction; drop style virtues such as elegance.

source: Bonawitz & Lombrozo (2012) Occam's rattle: children's use of simplicity and probability to constrain inference, Developmental Psychology
finding: Search snippet: children preferred one-cause over two-cause explanations but also reacted to the probability of competing explanations.
numbers: None seen.
limits: Snippet only; the page returned a bot check. Citation details of the snippet not verified.
agent_relevance: The simplicity-plus-probability pattern appears early in development, so likely deep and also present in training text.

source: Douven (2013), Douven & Wenmackers (2017) Inference to the best explanation versus Bayes's rule in a social setting, BJPS; EcoRatExRe preprint (hal-02869743)
finding: Search snippets: the explanationist rule has an adjustable parameter and the best speed versus accuracy balance depends on context; explanationist agents are faster to the truth but slightly worse on Brier score under certain evidence.
numbers: None seen. The fetch was blocked by a bot check.
limits: Not opened. Need the paper for parameters and exact conditions.
agent_relevance: The bonus should be small, and removed when time allows more tests.
